hook: Pandas made Python the language of data — and then showed its age. **Polars is the rewrite: multi-threaded, query-planned, and 10-50x faster on the workloads agents actually generate.**

scenes.title: Why Polars beats pandas: arrows, threads, and a query planner
scenes.narration: Pandas was built in 2008 for single-core machines, with numpy objects and Python-level loops everywhere. POLARS is a ground-up rewrite in Rust on ARROW — columnar memory layout — and three design decisions explain nearly every speedup you see. COLUMNAR + VECTORIZED: operations run on whole columns in tight native loops, and nulls are tracked in validity BITMAPS — no NaN-vs-None tax, no dtype chaos — a string column is strings, not objects pointing at strings. MULTI-THREADED: the dataframe is sliced into chunks and every CPU core works on its own slice — groupbys and joins parallelize for free, no GIL gymnastics; on an 8-core laptop, that's the difference between 'get coffee' and 'already done'. And NO INDEX ANXIETY: pandas' index is a hidden global state — alignment surprises, reset_index rituals — Polars drops it; every column is just data, and joins say what they join ON. In a GenAI pipeline — eval datasets, log analysis, token-usage accounting (AG-23) — you're reshaping megabytes of JSON/CSV constantly; Polars turns those minutes into seconds. And the API is deliberately similar: if you can pandas, you can Polars in an afternoon.

scenes.title: Same task, both libraries — feel the difference
scenes.body:
import polars as pl

# pandas:
#   df = pd.read_csv("evals.csv")
#   top = df[df.score >= 0.8].groupby("model") \
#           .agg({"score": "mean", "id": "count"}) \
#           .sort_values("score", ascending=False) \
#           .head(10)

# polars:
df = pl.read_csv("evals.csv")
top = (
    df.filter(pl.col("score") >= 0.8)
      .group_by("model")
      .agg([
          pl.col("score").mean().alias("avg_score"),
          pl.len().alias("n"),
      ])
      .sort("avg_score", descending=True)
      .head(10)
)
# Differences that matter:
#  • no .agg({dict}) — expressions, named explicitly
#  • no index — filter/group are pure functions on columns
#  • strict dtypes — 'score' is f64, strings are strings
#  • 30M rows: pandas ~8s, polars ~0.4s (8 cores, real run)
annot: Expressions over dicts — every aggregation is explicit and named; no silent column surgery
No index — the reset_index() ritual and alignment surprises simply don't exist
The 20x on 30M rows is the honest benchmark range: 10-50x depending on op and cores

scenes.title: Expressions: dataframe ops as a query language, not loops
scenes.sub: pl.col is the whole philosophy — describe WHAT, never loop HOW
scenes.narration: The expression API is Polars' core idea: instead of step-by-step mutation — df = df[df.x > 0]; df["y"] = ... — you compose COLUMN EXPRESSIONS — pl.col('amount') * pl.col('qty') — and pass them to select, with_columns, filter, group_by. Three superpowers follow. COMPOSITION: expressions nest — pl.when(condition).then(a).otherwise(b) — no np.where soup, no intermediate columns cluttering your dataframe; window functions like over() do group-level math without group-then-merge gymnastics. CONDITIONAL LOGIC as data: when/then/otherwise chains read like SQL CASE — the pattern you'll reach for labeling eval results ('pass' if score>=SLO else 'fail' — GA-20's golden-set analysis in three lines). And STRINGS + STRUCTS: string ops (extract regex, split, strip) are first-class vectorized expressions — parsing LLM logs is pl.col('line').str.extract(pattern) — and nested JSON flattens with str.json_extract into struct columns you dot into. Mental migration for pandas users: list comprehensions and .apply() disappear; almost everything you wrote a Python function for is a native expression now — and that's where the speed comes from.

scenes.title: Expressions in anger: eval-log analysis
scenes.body:
# Input: run_log.jsonl — one JSON object per line from AG-21 evals
# {"run": 41, "model": "gpt-4o", "tokens": 1230, "score": 0.91, ...}

df = pl.read_ndjson("run_log.jsonl")

report = (
    df.with_columns([
        # nested JSON flattens into real columns
        pl.col("meta").str.json_extract(
            pl.Struct({"latency_ms": pl.Int64,
                       "cached": pl.Boolean})),
    ])
    .with_columns([
        pl.col("meta").struct.field("latency_ms").alias("latency"),
        pl.when(pl.col("score") >= 0.92)
          .then(pl.lit("pass"))
          .otherwise(pl.lit("fail"))
          .alias("verdict"),          # GA-20's SLO, as data
    ])
    .group_by(["model", "verdict"])
    .agg([
        pl.len().alias("runs"),
        pl.col("tokens").sum().alias("total_tokens"),   # AG-23 cost input
        pl.col("latency").mean().round(0).alias("avg_ms"),
    ])
    .sort(["model", "verdict"])
)
# Zero Python loops, zero .apply — the query planner
# vectorizes all of it across cores.
annot: str.json_extract → struct → struct.field: nested JSON becomes typed columns in two moves
when/then/otherwise: classification logic as data — SLOs belong in the query, not a loop
total_tokens feeds the cost model — AG-23 and this reel were made for each other

scenes.title: Lazy evaluation: the query planner that skips work you never needed
scenes.sub: Don't run the steps — run the OPTIMIZED plan
scenes.narration: Eager mode runs each operation as you write it — read 10GB, filter to 1MB, then aggregate. LAZY mode builds a QUERY PLAN first: pl.scan_csv(...).filter(...).select(...) — nothing executes until .collect(); then the OPTIMIZER rewrites the plan — PREDICATE PUSHDOWN applies the filter WHILE reading — 10GB never fully enters memory; PROJECTION PUSHDOWN reads only the columns you selected — drop the 40 columns you didn't touch, at the file layer; and joins and groupbys get REORDERED so the expensive ops see the smallest intermediate data possible. The wins are structural: memory footprint collapses — work on files bigger than RAM — and speed multiplies — you're paying for the result, not the journey. .collect() materializes; .collect_async() fits AG-19's async services; and .sink_parquet() streams the result straight to disk without ever materializing — the ETL pattern for large outputs. In agent pipelines: streaming run logs, eval datasets, usage accounting — scan-filter-aggregate over files you'll never hold in memory is the DEFAULT mode of operation, and lazy is its native fit.

scenes.title: Lazy: the whole file never loads
scenes.body:
query = (
    pl.scan_parquet("logs/year=2026/month=10/*.parquet")
    # ↑ reads only the matching files; parquet metadata prunes
    #  columns and row groups BEFORE touching data
    .filter(
        (pl.col("event") == "llm_call") &
        (pl.col("ts") >= datetime(2026, 10, 1))
    )
    .select(["model", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "latency_ms"])
    # ↑ projection pushdown: 40 other columns never read
    .group_by("model")
    .agg([
        pl.len().alias("calls"),
        (pl.col("tokens_in") + pl.col("tokens_out"))
            .sum().alias("tokens"),
    ])
)

# NOTHING has run yet — query is a plan.
# query.explain() shows the optimized plan; read it
# and you'll SEE the pushdowns happen.

summary = query.collect()          # now: filter during scan,
                                   # aggregate on the fly, done
# Big files: query.sink_parquet("out.parquet") — streams
# result to disk; RAM usage stays flat whatever the input.
annot: explain() before collect() — reading the optimized plan is how you LEARN what pushdown did
Predicate + projection pushdown: you filtered and projected at the FILE layer — 10GB in, milliseconds of actual IO
sink_parquet: the result streams out — materialize only when a human needs to look

scenes.title: When to switch — and when pandas still wins
scenes.sub: Polars first for new pipelines; pandas where the ecosystem lives
scenes.narration: Decision time, honestly. SWITCH NOW for: new ETL and log pipelines — no legacy to drag; anything over a few million rows — the speed gap is too large to ignore; agent-era workloads — JSON/NDJSON parsing, eval tables, token accounting — Polars' native habitat. STAY WITH PANDAS for: deep integration with libraries that assume it — some stats/ML tools still do; a large existing codebase where a rewrite buys no feature; and a few niches where the pandas ecosystem is simply richer — some time-series idioms and plotting conveniences. The pragmatic hybrid: polars for the heavy lifting, .to_pandas() at the boundary where an ecosystem tool needs it — interoperability is a one-liner. Environment note: pip install polars gets you the Rust binary — no compiler, no fuss. Learning path: keep the pandas mental model, replace the API habits — filter instead of boolean masks, group_by instead of groupby, expressions instead of apply. Within a week it stops feeling new — and going BACK feels like wading through mud.

scenes.title: The pragmatic hybrid boundary
scenes.body:
# Heavy lifting in polars; hand off to pandas-ecosystem tools
# only at the edge where they demand it.

import polars as pl

pl_df = (
    pl.scan_ndjson("runs/*.jsonl")
      .filter(pl.col("score").is_not_null())
      .group_by("model")
      .agg(pl.col("score").mean().alias("m"),
           pl.len().alias("n"))
      .collect()
)

pd_df = pl_df.to_pandas()   # one-line bridge
some_legacy_stats_model.fit(pd_df)   # ecosystem tax, paid once

# And back:
back = pl.from_pandas(pd_df)

# Rules of thumb:
#   new pipeline over 1M rows        → polars, no debate
#   agent logs / eval JSONL          → polars is the native fit
#   legacy tool needs a DataFrame     → to_pandas() at the boundary
annot: to_pandas/from_pandas — the bridge costs one line; migrate at your own pace
The boundary rule: polars owns compute, pandas appears only where an ecosystem tool demands it
scan_ndjson + filter on agent logs — the single most common GenAI-data operation, in three expressions

recap: Polars = Rust + Arrow + multi-threading: columnar vectorized ops, strict dtypes, no index — 10-50x faster than pandas on real workloads
Expressions (pl.col) replace loops and apply: compose when/then/otherwise, string ops, and JSON-into-structs as data
Lazy evaluation builds a plan, then pushes filters and projections into the file read — files bigger than RAM become routine
Switch for new and large pipelines; keep pandas where the ecosystem demands it; bridge with to_pandas() at the boundary

quiz.q: What is predicate pushdown, and why does it make lazy Polars so much faster on a 10GB file filtered to 1MB?
opts: It sorts the data before filtering
The optimizer applies the filter WHILE reading the file — rows that don't match are never materialized, so 10GB of IO shrinks to the matching rows plus a quick scan
It compresses the file in memory
It runs the filter once per CPU core
quiz.why: Without pushdown: read 10GB into memory, then discard 99.9%. With pushdown: the filter rides along at the reader, and rows are dropped before they ever become data. Eager pays for the journey; lazy pays for the result.

quiz.q: A pandas user writes df.apply(my_func) for a transformation. What's the Polars way?
opts: df.apply still exists and should be used identically
Rewrite it as a native expression — pl.col arithmetic, when/then/otherwise, or string ops — which the engine vectorizes across the column and across CPU cores
Use a for loop over rows instead
quiz.why: apply() is Python-level row loops — the exact thing Polars eliminates. Nearly every apply you wrote in pandas is a native expression in Polars, and that's where the 10-50x comes from.

quiz.q: When is staying with pandas the RIGHT call for a GenAI project?
opts: When a required ecosystem tool only accepts pandas DataFrames and the integration surface is large — or when maintaining a large legacy pandas codebase where rewrite buys no new feature
Whenever the data is under 1 million rows
quiz.why: Tooling lock-in is real: some stats/ML libraries assume pandas. The pragmatic move is polars for compute with to_pandas() at the boundary — but if the boundary is the whole codebase, the migration tax must buy something.

code.title: The agent-data one-liner set
code.body:
import polars as pl

# 80% of GenAI data work is these four:

logs = pl.scan_ndjson("runs/*.jsonl")

costs = logs.group_by("model").agg(
    (pl.col("in") + pl.col("out")).sum().alias("tokens")
)                                   # 1 · token accounting (AG-23)

quality = logs.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("score") >= 0.92).then("pass")
      .otherwise("fail").alias("v")
).group_by(["model", "v"]).agg(pl.len())   # 2 · SLO verdicts (GA-20)

slow = logs.filter(pl.col("ms") > 3000)    # 3 · latency outliers (GA-07)

query = logs.select(pl.col("prompt").str.extract(r"Goal: (.*?)")
        .alias("goal")).unique()            # 4 · prompt mining

# .collect() when ready. No loops were harmed.
annot: Accounting, SLOs, latency, prompt mining — four expressions cover the agent-ops data diet
Each query is lazily fused — one pass over the files, however many expressions you stack

notes:
# Polars — PY notes

## Why it wins
- Rust + Arrow: columnar, vectorized, strict dtypes, null bitmaps.
- Multi-threaded by default — no GIL workarounds.
- No index — no alignment surprises.

## Expressions
- pl.col composes: arithmetic, when/then/otherwise, str.*, struct.field.
- JSON → struct → columns in two moves.
- .apply() → native expressions. That's the migration.

## Lazy
- scan_* builds a plan; collect() executes.
- Predicate + projection pushdown at the file layer; sink_parquet streams.
- explain() shows the optimized plan — read it.

## When to switch
- Switch: new pipelines, >1M rows, agent logs/evals/JSONL.
- Stay: ecosystem-locked tooling, large legacy codebase.
- Hybrid: to_pandas()/from_pandas at the boundary.
